content: Salicylic acid is an FDA-approved anti-acne agent used for the treatment of acne. It is also indicated for the relief of itching, irritation, redness, and scaling associated with conditions such as psoriasis, eczema, and seborrheic dermatitis. Common adverse reactions include hypersensitivity reactions and salicylate toxicity. For adult patients, salicylic acid is used in the following ways: For acne treatment, it helps to keep the skin clear of new acne blemishes. For relief of symptoms associated with psoriasis, eczema, and seborrheic dermatitis, it is applied topically in concentrations of 3% to 6%. For hyperkeratotic skin disorders, a gel containing 5% to 10% salicylic acid is applied topically to the affected area, with occlusion at night. Alternatively, a shampoo formulation can be used by wetting the hair, applying the product to the scalp, working it into a lather, and rinsing. This process can be repeated as needed until the condition clears. For wart removal, salicylic acid is applied topically once or twice daily in concentrations of 5% to 40% for up to 12 weeks. There is limited information regarding off-label, non-guideline-supported uses of salicylic acid in adult patients. For pediatric patients, there is limited information regarding FDA-labeled indications, dosages, and off-label uses of salicylic acid. Similarly, there is no FDA guidance on its use in specific populations, including pregnant women, nursing mothers, pediatric patients, geriatric patients, specific gender or racial populations, or patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Additionally, there is no guidance on its use in immunocompromised patients. Salicylic acid is contraindicated for external use only. Contact with the eyes should be avoided, and if contact occurs, the area should be rinsed thoroughly with water. It should not be used without consulting a doctor if the condition affects a large portion of the body. If the condition worsens or does not improve after directed use, a physician should be consulted. Prolonged use without medical advice is not recommended. Adverse reactions reported include hypersensitivity reactions and salicylate toxicity. There is limited information available regarding clinical trial experiences, postmarketing experiences, and drug interactions involving salicylic acid. The mechanism of action of salicylic acid involves several pathways. It exerts anti-inflammatory effects by suppressing the activity of cyclooxygenase (COX), an enzyme responsible for producing pro-inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins. Unlike most NSAIDs, salicylic acid does not directly inhibit COX but suppresses its expression through an unclear mechanism. Salicylic acid also activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which may contribute to its anticancer and antidiabetic effects. It is thought to mediate antidiabetic effects by inducing allosteric conformational changes that increase phosphorylation levels. Additionally, salicylic acid uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, altering cellular energy status and potentially influencing AMPK activity. Even in AMPK knockout mice, salicylic acid demonstrates antidiabetic effects, suggesting additional unidentified mechanisms of action. There is limited information available regarding the structure, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology of salicylic acid. Clinical studies and details on how the drug is supplied or stored are also limited. For patient counseling, affected areas should be washed thoroughly with soap and water, patted dry, and the cream applied to the affected area one to four times daily or as directed by a physician. The interaction between alcohol and salicylic acid has not been established. Patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while using this medication. One brand name for salicylic acid is ALA-SEPTIC®. There is limited information regarding look-alike drug names for salicylic acid.
